name: Glaucous-Blue
lede: Glaucous-Blue is a soft green-blue that Ridgway attached to the family word glaucous as early as 1886, a pairing both the ISCC-NBS and Maerz and Paul dictionaries kept.

sections.title: A family word since 1886
sections.body:
Ridgway's earlier 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors* already carried Glaucous-Blue, and his fuller 1912 standards placed it on plate XXXIV, hue 43 double-prime, tone b [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary repeats it on plate 36, swatch I3, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it as a light greenish blue, block 172 [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[pastel-turquoise]], [[greenish-blue]] and [[greyish-blue]], at 3.9, 
The closest common color word in our library is [[ash|Ash]], about twelve units away in CIEDE2000, a looser match than most of the names we carry [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within six units of Glaucous-Blue covers at least five percent of the canvas in 243 of our 23,781 paintings, 1.02 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 150 [2]. That ranks it ahead of 66 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It is most common in the Impressionist movement, seven of 140 paintings there, 3.5 times the expected rate, and it most often plays a hidden color, lowest in a painting's own lightness order, in 40 percent of its 150 appearances [2].

No single painter stands out against the museum baselines, though Eugène Boudin carries it most often, in four of his 33 paintings here [2]. The earliest matching painting dates to 1375, 511 years before Ridgway's first record of the name in 1886 — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the color existed as a dye or pigment that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
